summary: Vaidas Razgaitis from Higharc's labs team addresses the challenge of bridging ML research with production engineering. Higharc operates in home building and spatial reasoning, requiring multidisciplinary AI including computer vision for parsing hand-sketched floor plans, reasoning agents for agentic experiences, custom transformers, and diffusion models for image generation. The fundamental problem is the baton pass between ML researchers (versed in latest papers but inexperienced with production-grade APIs) and software engineers (robust systems builders unfamiliar with ML methodology). Razgaitis frames this as a systems and process problem with three focus areas. First, research legibility: ML researchers must produce a Research Prototype Taxonomy (RPT) document—akin to a technical design document with ML-specific twists. It contains six parts: domain context (data representations like parquet diagrams, circulation graphs, embedding models), business goal justification, type safety contracts between repos, persistence layer mapping, overall system architecture (workflow vs. chaining, external LLM calls), and decomposition/merge strategy. Second, code structure: Higharc uses a separate Python-based mono repo from the core product, organized as cleanly isolated, fully decoupled microservices with a one-to-one researcher-to-microservice ratio. A gateway guards requests in a Docker bridge network, routing client API calls to appropriate microservices. Each microservice follows a layered architecture (API layer, business logic, data layer) with FastAPI applications, controllers, and routers. The repo includes GitHub Actions for CI/CD, Jupyter notebooks on Modal for GPU compute, and a CLI tooling layer. Third, decomposition and PR review: large research prototypes are sliced along studied axes into a dependency graph, then decomposed using Graphite for stacked diffs, enabling asynchronous review by domain specialists. The RPT document informs decomposition strategy. Razgaitis also provides diagnostic frameworks for each focus area: for research legibility, check if team members know where to concentrate efforts; for code repository, verify clear placement buckets and templates exist; for decomposition, assess whether PRs can be properly reviewed, whether timelines and delivery dates can be consistently estimated, and whether the right subject matter experts are identified for review and productionizing. Issues in these areas point to problems in research coordination, handoff processes, or the hosting codebase. He concludes by inviting audience members to compare notes and trade ideas on accelerating research-to-production workflows.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The research-to-production gap is fundamentally a handoff problem between ML researchers and software engineers with complementary but non-overlapping skill sets

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Razgaitis introduces Higharc's labs team and its multidisciplinary AI work in home building. He frames the core problem: ML researchers lack production engineering experience while software engineers lack ML methodology familiarity, creating a handoff challenge.

sections.title: Research Legibility - RPT Document
sections.summary: Details the Research Prototype Taxonomy document with six parts: domain context, business goal, type safety, persistence layer, system architecture, and decomposition/merge strategy. References Pragmatic Engineer blog on technical design documents.

sections.title: Code Structure - Mono Repo
sections.summary: Describes the Python-based mono repo of decoupled microservices with one-to-one researcher ratio, gateway routing in Docker bridge network, layered architecture with FastAPI, GitHub Actions CI/CD, Modal GPU compute, and CLI tooling.

sections.title: Decomposition and PR Review
sections.summary: Explains using Graphite for stacked diffs to decompose large monolithic prototypes, enabling asynchronous review by domain specialists on specific slices informed by the RPT document.

sections.title: Diagnostic Frameworks
sections.summary: Introduces diagnostic questions for each focus area: whether task ownership is clear (research legibility), whether placement buckets and templates exist (code repository), whether PRs can be properly reviewed, whether timelines and delivery dates can be consistently estimated, and whether the right subject matter experts are identified for review and productionizing (decomposition). Issues in these areas point to problems in research coordination, handoff processes, or the hosting codebase.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Razgaitis concludes by expressing enthusiasm for accelerating research-to-production workflows and invites audience members interested in the topic to compare notes and trade ideas anytime.
